title: Ramadan: the family
hookLine: iftars with family, children's first fasts

cards: A small toy made of wool. Al-Rubayyi' bint Mu'awwidh, a woman of Madinah, describes it in Sahih al-Bukhari. Her people fasted, she says, and had their small children fast too.
And they made toys out of wool for them. When one of the children cried for food, they'd hand over the toy, and the child would play with it until it was time to break the fast. No lecture.
No scolding. A toy, and a little longer to wait.

teach.b: First, be honest about the report. Al-Rubayyi' is speaking about the fast of Ashura, not Ramadan. But it gives a picture of how children were brought into a fast: gently, with play, alongside the adults.
Children aren't required to fast before they come of age, as you met earlier on the path, so a child's first fast is practice, not duty.
Some families start with half a day, or a fast that ends at lunch, and make a fuss of the child at sunset. Second, the moment the fast breaks.
In al-Bukhari the Prophet, peace be upon him, says people will remain in good as long as they hurry to break the fast. When the sun goes down, you eat.
And in a report in Abu Dawud, Anas describes how: with fresh dates before the prayer, and if there were none, dried dates, and if there were none, a few sips of water.
So the iftar starts small and sweet, and for some families the big meal comes after. Third, the table.
For some families, iftar is the one meal of the day when everyone is home at the same minute, because the sun decides the time, not anyone's schedule.
Grandparents, cousins, the kid who just finished a half-day fast and wants everyone to know. Put the toy and the date side by side. Both are small.
Both say the fast is hard, and the family's job is to make it bearable, together, until the moment it's sweet.

how: Muslim families gather for iftar at sunset during Ramadan, breaking the fast with dates and water as a report in Abu Dawud describes; children aren't required to fast before maturity, and some families let them practice with partial fasts.

o: a fast only adults keep, with children left out of it
the fasting month, kept together at the family iftar table
a month of feasting at home before the year's long fast

games.q: the family fasts — tap the pairs.
p: made toys of wool for fasting children

s: children must fast the whole of Ramadan from an early age
children aren't required to fast before they come of age; their fasts are practice.
the Prophet said people remain in good as long as they hurry to break the fast
it's in al-Bukhari: when the sun goes down, eat.
the toys of wool in al-Rubayyi's report were for Ramadan
she was speaking of the fast of Ashura.

games.q: you're a mother in Madinah. your small child is fasting with the family, and at midday starts crying for food. what do you do?
o: give them a toy of wool to play with until it's time to break the fast.
tell them fasting isn't for children and send them away.
games.why: al-Rubayyi' says they made toys of wool and gave one to a crying child until it was time to break the fast.

practice: Bring to mind a child in your life, a son or daughter, a niece, a neighbor's kid, or the child you once were, and think of one way they could share in something you care about, sized to them: a job at the table, handing out the dates, saying the first thing at a meal.
Picture their face when they're trusted with it. If you pray, you can remember that child by name.

wordCard.voice: Ramadan. The month of fasting, kept at home around the iftar table, where children practice small fasts and the day breaks with dates. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: breaking the fast, and the meal at sunset.

carryVoice: Your line: the family fasts. Small and sweet, together. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1960 (al-Rubayyi' bint Mu'awwidh: children fasting, toys of wool)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1957 (people remain in good as long as they hasten the iftar)
Sunan Abu Dawud 2356 (Anas: fresh dates, then dried dates, then sips of water)
